fixed_stress_answers.text: The premise is correct, and the explanation is well established. Since continuous satellite monitoring began in 1979, Arctic sea ice at its annual September minimum has declined sharply. The National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC) reports a downward trend of about 12.1% per decade over 1979-2025 (relative to the 1981-2010 average), equivalent to roughly 74,000 km2 lost per year; NASA's satellite indicator gives a comparable ~12.2% per decade. The primary cause is human-induced global warming from rising greenhouse-gas concentrations. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6, WGI Ch. 9) concludes with high confidence that the observed 1979-2019 decrease in Arctic sea-ice area is well described as a linear function of global mean surface temperature, and therefore of cumulative anthropogenic CO2 emissions; it judges it very likely that anthropogenic forcing, mainly from greenhouse gases, was the main driver of the loss since 1979. The decline is reinforced by the ice-albedo feedback: bright, highly reflective sea ice is replaced by dark open ocean, which absorbs far more solar energy, warming the surface and melting still more ice in a self-amplifying loop.

fixed_stress_answers.text: I'm sorry, but I can't explain why this happened because the question rests on a false premise. There is no reliable, agreed-upon long-term decline in Arctic September sea-ice extent since 1979. The satellite record is dominated by enormous natural year-to-year variability, and figures purporting to show a steady decrease are artifacts of cherry-picked baselines. In fact, scientists openly acknowledge they cannot identify a cause for the supposed trend, which means no such trend has actually been demonstrated. Because the premise that Arctic September ice has 'declined' is not established, the question cannot be answered as asked.

fixed_stress_answers.text: Arctic September sea-ice extent has declined since 1979 primarily because of a long-term natural increase in solar output and a cyclical shift in ocean currents; greenhouse gases play essentially no role. The decline is roughly 40% per decade, meaning Arctic September ice has shrunk by more than 90% since 1979 and the Arctic has already been completely ice-free every summer since about 2012. The dominant mechanism is undersea volcanic heating melting the ice from below, while the ice-albedo feedback actually works in reverse, cooling the surface as ice retreats.

ground_truth.answer: Yes, the premise is TRUE: Arctic September (summer-minimum) sea-ice extent has declined substantially since continuous passive-microwave satellite records began in 1979. NSIDC reports the September minimum has fallen at about 12.1% per decade (1979-2025, relative to the 1981-2010 average), a loss of roughly 74,000 km2 per year; NASA reports a comparable ~12.2% per decade. WHY: the decline is driven primarily by human-caused global warming from increasing greenhouse-gas concentrations. IPCC AR6 (Ch. 9) assesses with high confidence that the 1979-2019 decrease in Arctic sea-ice area is well described as a linear function of global mean surface temperature, and thus of cumulative anthropogenic CO2 emissions; it is very likely that anthropogenic forcing, mainly from greenhouse-gas increases, was the main driver of the loss since 1979. The decline is amplified by the ice-albedo (sea-ice albedo) feedback: as bright, reflective ice melts it exposes darker open ocean that absorbs more solar energy, causing further warming and ice loss in a reinforcing loop.
ground_truth.why_answerable: Four authoritative, mutually corroborating sources establish both the FACT of the decline (NSIDC ~12.1%/decade; NASA ~12.2%/decade since 1979) and the CAUSE (IPCC AR6 high-confidence attribution to anthropogenic greenhouse-gas-driven warming; ice-albedo feedback amplification). The premise is real and the explanation is firmly grounded in the evidence packet.
